blocks.text: **Diabetes mellitus** is a syndrome of **chronic hyperglycaemia** caused by **insulin deficiency, insulin resistance, or both**. It carries **acute metabolic** complications and long-term **microvascular** (eye, kidney, nerve) and **macrovascular** complications. **Type 1** is mainly **autoimmune destruction of β cells**, which leaves a severe insulin deficit. **Type 2** combines **insulin resistance** with β cells that **cannot secrete enough insulin** to overcome it.

The diagnostic glucose cut-offs were set where untreated hyperglycaemia starts to carry a real risk of **microvascular disease, especially retinopathy**. Lesser degrees (**pre-diabetes**) mainly raise **macrovascular** risk and the chance of future diabetes.

blocks.title: Aetiological classification (Davidson Box 20.9)
rows: Insulin resistance + relative insulin deficiency; about 90% of all diabetes
Pancreatitis, pancreatectomy, carcinoma, cystic fibrosis, haemochromatosis
Glucocorticoids, thiazide diuretics, phenytoin; also atypical antipsychotics and HIV protease inhibitors

blocks.title: Classical type 1 vs type 2 (Davidson Box 20.12)
rows: How long symptoms last before diagnosis

blocks.title: Special types worth knowing
items: **MODY**: autosomal dominant, non-insulin-requiring diabetes diagnosed **before 25** in at least one family member. **Glucokinase MODY** → mild, stable fasting hyperglycaemia that **needs no treatment**. **HNF1α / HNF4α MODY** → **very sensitive to sulphonylureas**. **HNF1β MODY** → **renal cysts** and genital tract malformations.
**LADA**: an adult with **high-titre islet antibodies (usually GAD)** who does not need insulin at first; treated like type 2 initially but **progresses to insulin sooner**.
**Permanent neonatal diabetes**: most often **activating KATP-channel mutations (KIR6.2 / SUR1)**; over 90% can switch from insulin to **oral sulphonylureas**.

**Ketosis-prone type 2 ("Flatbush") diabetes**: presents in **DKA**, classically described in African American people; needs insulin at first, but β-cell function often recovers so **metformin can replace insulin after ~3 months**.

blocks.text: **DKA does not prove type 1.** Ketosis-prone type 2 diabetes presents in DKA, and LADA can look like type 2 at first. Label the type on antibodies, C-peptide and course, not on the first presentation alone.

blocks.title: Epidemiology
items: About **415 million** adults (~10%) had diabetes in 2015, projected to reach **642 million by 2040**. The growth is almost all **type 2**, driven by obesity, inactivity, urbanisation and ageing.
**Type 2 ≈ 90%** of all diabetes, **type 1 ≈ 5–10%**. About three-quarters of people with type 2 live in low- and middle-income countries, and many cases go **undiagnosed** for years.
**Type 1** incidence is rising and is highest near the poles: **Finland > 60 per 100 000 per year** vs about 0.1 per 100 000 in China, India and Venezuela. More cases are diagnosed in **winter**.
**Type 2** affects ~10% of UK people over 65; over 70% of cases arise **after age 50**. A **BMI > 30 kg/m²** raises the risk about **10-fold**.

blocks.title: Type 1: risk in first-degree relatives (Davidson Box 20.6)

blocks.text: **Type 1 aetiology:** polygenic susceptibility, chiefly **HLA DR3 and/or DR4** (travelling with DQA1/DQB1), meets an **environmental trigger**. Proposed triggers include **viruses** (mumps, Coxsackie B4, congenital rubella, CMV, EBV, retroviruses), dietary nitrosamines, early **cow's milk** exposure, the **hygiene hypothesis** and **low vitamin D**. None is proven to be causal. Despite the genetics, **80–85% of new cases have no family history**.

**Type 1 pathogenesis:** T-cell-mediated **insulitis** destroys β cells progressively while **α and δ cells are spared**. Islet autoantibodies appear first, then loss of first-phase insulin secretion and impaired glucose tolerance. Overt diabetes appears only when **80–90% of β-cell function is lost**.

**Type 2 pathogenesis:** **insulin resistance** comes first. Insulin fails to suppress hepatic glucose output, muscle takes up less glucose and adipose lipolysis is not suppressed. The pancreas compensates with **hyperinsulinaemia** until susceptible β cells fail. About **50% of β-cell function is already lost at diagnosis**, and **islet amyloid** is the most consistent histological change. Raised **glucagon** and a diminished **incretin effect** add to the hyperglycaemia. Hyperglycaemia and FFAs then injure β cells further (**glucolipotoxicity**).

blocks.title: Type 2 risk factors
items: **Genetics**: strong. Monozygotic twin concordance approaches 100%, and **TCF7L2** has the largest effect among common variants.
**Obesity** (the greatest modifiable risk, especially central fat), overeating and **physical inactivity**.
**Increasing age**.
**High-risk ethnicity**: e.g. Native Americans (~33% prevalence in the USA), South Asian, Chinese and Black populations.

blocks.text: **Metabolic syndrome** (insulin resistance syndrome): type 2 diabetes clusters with **hypertension**, **dyslipidaemia** (high triglycerides, low HDL, small dense LDL), **NAFLD** and, in women, **PCOS**. Visceral fat releasing **FFAs and adipokines** drives hepatic insulin resistance.

**Acute effects of insulin deficiency:** hyperglycaemia causes **glycosuria and osmotic diuresis**, leading to dehydration. Unrestrained **lipolysis** delivers FFAs to the liver for **ketogenesis**, causing **metabolic acidosis**. H⁺ drives **K⁺ out of cells**, and secondary hyperaldosteronism increases **urinary K⁺ loss**.
**Why type 2 rarely causes ketoacidosis:** suppressing lipolysis needs only a little insulin. The residual insulin in type 2 does this, so marked weight loss and ketosis are unusual.

blocks.note: Look at: the time course of type 1 — insulitis, then autoantibodies, then loss of first-phase insulin release, then IGT, then overt diabetes as β-cell mass falls
Look at: the two arms of insulin deficiency — hyperglycaemia → osmotic diuresis, and lipolysis → ketogenesis → acidosis, with K⁺ loss

blocks.text: **New diabetes in an older patient with weight loss and poor appetite** should raise suspicion of **pancreatic carcinoma**. **Alcohol-related chronic pancreatitis** is a common but often missed cause, and usually ends up needing insulin.

**Twin concordance figures differ between books.** Step-Up quotes ~50% for type 1 and ~90% for type 2. Davidson gives **30–50%** for identical twins with type 1 and says type 2 concordance **approaches 100%**. Use Davidson's figures; the key point is that the **genetic component is stronger in type 2**.

blocks.title: Symptoms of hyperglycaemia and their mechanism
rows: Loss of insulin's anabolic action (fat and protein breakdown)

blocks.title: How the types usually present
rows: Days to a few weeks, sometimes after an illness
Thirst, polyuria, weight loss, infections, or **DKA**
Incidental finding, screening, or a **complication** (MI, stroke, claudication, neuropathy, retinopathy)
> 80% overweight (often central), ≥ 50% hypertensive, up to 25% already have complications

blocks.title: Examining a patient with diabetes
items: **Hands**: limited joint mobility (cheiroarthropathy, the **"prayer sign"**), Dupuytren's contracture, carpal tunnel syndrome.
**Blood pressure**.
**Skin and axillae**: **acanthosis nigricans** (marker of insulin resistance), necrobiosis lipoidica, xanthelasma, vitiligo.
**Eyes**: visual acuity, cataract, fundoscopy through dilated pupils.
**Injection sites**: **lipohypertrophy**.
**Feet**: callus, clawed toes, ulcers, deformity (Charcot), pulses, **monofilament** sensation and ankle reflexes.

blocks.note: Look at: acanthosis nigricans, the prayer sign, necrobiosis lipoidica, lipohypertrophy, Charcot foot and neuropathic ulcer

blocks.text: Up to a quarter of people with type 2 already have complications at diagnosis, so the disease may first be found by an **optometrist or podiatrist**, or after an **MI or stroke**.
A young person with type 1 can deteriorate within days. The first presentation may be **DKA**, sometimes triggered by an intercurrent illness, rather than a clinic visit with thirst.

blocks.title: Diagnostic criteria (any one; see the confirmation rule below)
Confirmation rules
items: **Symptomatic** patient: one diagnostic plasma glucose is enough.
**Asymptomatic** patient: needs **two** diagnostic results, ideally the same test repeated (Step-Up repeats HbA1c after more than 3 months).
**Never diagnose on capillary (finger-prick) readings.**
**OGTT**: fasting sample, a 75 g glucose drink, then plasma glucose 2 hours later. It is the preferred test in **pregnancy**.

blocks.title: Pre-diabetes (intermediate hyperglycaemia)
rows: Fasting 6.1 to < 7.0 mmol/L (ADA uses ≥ 5.6 mmol/L, i.e. 100–125 mg/dL)
About 1–5% per year progress to type 2; cardiovascular risk is also raised

blocks.text: **Do not use HbA1c to diagnose** suspected **type 1**, rapid-onset symptomatic hyperglycaemia, or diabetes in **pregnancy**. HbA1c reads **falsely low in anaemia and pregnancy** and is **unreliable with uraemia, haemolysis or a haemoglobinopathy**. Fructosamine can be used for monitoring instead.

**Glycosuria is not diagnostic.** Its commonest cause is a **low renal threshold** (benign renal glycosuria, common in pregnancy and the young). In older people the threshold rises, so glycosuria may be absent despite high glucose.

blocks.title: Tests that refine the diagnosis
rows: Marks **endogenous** insulin secretion, even on injected insulin: very low in long-standing type 1, very high in severe insulin resistance
GAD, IA-2, insulin and ZnT8 antibodies support type 1 or LADA
< 0.6 mmol/L normal; > 3.0 mmol/L with glucose > 10 mmol/L suggests DKA
Nitroprusside detects **acetoacetate only**, not β-hydroxybutyrate (the main DKA ketone)
Urea, creatinine and electrolytes, lipids, liver and thyroid function, ketones, urine protein (ACR)

blocks.note: Look at: the new-hyperglycaemia algorithm — unwell or ketotic → DKA/HHS pathway; well → decide type 1 vs type 2 vs other using antibodies, C-peptide and history

blocks.text: About **1 in 20 people with type 1 have coeliac disease** on biopsy. Type 1 also clusters with thyroid disease, Addison's, pernicious anaemia and vitiligo. Many countries screen routinely for coeliac disease.

blocks.title: DKA vs HHS
rows: ≥ 11 mmol/L (can be near-normal: pregnancy, SGLT2 inhibitors)

blocks.title: DKA: precipitants and features
items: **Precipitants**: missed or inadequate insulin, infection, inflammation (e.g. pancreatitis), infarction (MI, stroke), drugs (steroids, **SGLT2 inhibitors**), intoxication.
**Features**: nausea and vomiting, **abdominal pain** that can mimic an acute abdomen, **Kussmaul breathing**, ketotic (fruity) breath, dehydration with tachycardia and hypotension, drowsiness.
**Leucocytosis** is a stress response and **fever may be absent** despite infection. Amylase can rise without pancreatitis.

blocks.title: Markers of severe DKA (Davidson Box 20.15)
items: Ketones > 6 mmol/L, bicarbonate < 5 mmol/L, pH < 7.0
Admission **K⁺ < 3.5 mmol/L**
GCS < 12, SpO₂ < 92% on air, systolic BP < 90 mmHg, pulse > 100 or < 60
Anion gap > 16 mmol/L

blocks.text: **Every DKA patient is total-body potassium depleted**, even if plasma K⁺ is high at first. K⁺ falls sharply once insulin and fluids start, so monitor and replace it from the outset.

blocks.title: DKA: first hours (Davidson Box 20.16, JBDS)
rows: 0.9% saline **1 L over 60 min** if SBP > 90; if SBP < 90, **500 mL over 10–15 min** then reassess
**Fixed-rate IV soluble insulin 0.1 U/kg/hr**; continue the usual SC long-acting (basal) analogue
K⁺ > 5.5 → none; **3.5–5.5 → 40 mmol/L**; < 3.5 → senior review, more K⁺ needed
Glucose falls 3–6 mmol/L/hr **or** ketones fall ≥ 0.5 mmol/L/hr
Add **10% glucose 125 mL/hr** when glucose < 14 mmol/L, continuing saline and insulin
By 24 h: ketones < 0.3 mmol/L and venous bicarbonate > 18 mmol/L
Restart SC insulin when eating; stop IV insulin **30 min after** the SC short-acting dose

blocks.text: **Unit and threshold differences.** US texts (Step-Up, Pocket) define DKA with bicarbonate < 18 and glucose usually > 250 mg/dL. Their potassium rule is to **hold insulin if K⁺ < 3.3**, add K⁺ at 3.3–5.3 and give none above 5.3, and they add 5% dextrose at about 200–250 mg/dL. For our exams follow **Davidson/JBDS**: bicarbonate < 15, K⁺ bands **3.5 / 5.5**, and 10% glucose below 14 mmol/L.

**IV bicarbonate is not recommended** in DKA. It can paradoxically worsen CSF acidosis and is linked to **cerebral oedema** in the young, the main cause of DKA death in children. Avoid lowering glucose too fast. Large saline volumes can also cause a **hyperchloraemic non-anion-gap acidosis**.

blocks.title: HHS management (Davidson Box 20.17)
items: Start with **0.9% saline alone** (1 L over the first hour); fluid losses can reach 10–12 L.
Aim for a gradual fall in osmolality of **3–8 mOsmol/kg/hr**; consider 0.45% saline only if osmolality is rising despite adequate fluid balance.
Insulin **0.05 U/kg/hr only if** ketones (3-hydroxybutyrate) > 1.0 mmol/L, or once glucose is falling **< 5 mmol/L/hr** despite adequate fluids.
Keep glucose **10–15 mmol/L** in the first 24 h; give **prophylactic LMWH** until discharge; check feet daily.

blocks.text: **Correct the sodium in hyperglycaemia.** Water moves out of cells and dilutes Na⁺. Davidson adds **1.6 mmol/L for each 5.55 mmol/L (100 mg/dL) of glucose** above normal (Pocket's formula uses 2.4). Total body sodium is not low.

**Urine ketone sticks can mislead.** Nitroprusside detects acetoacetate only. **β-hydroxybutyrate** is the main ketone in DKA, and in shock the balance shifts further towards it, so the dipstick can underestimate or miss ketosis. Measure **blood ketones**.

blocks.note: Look at: side-by-side DKA vs HHS — glucose, pH, ketones, osmolality, treatment and mortality

blocks.text: In people with diabetes, **hypoglycaemia is a blood glucose < 3.9 mmol/L (70 mg/dL)**. It is **severe** when someone else has to help with treatment. The main causes are **insulin** and **sulphonylureas**. Within **5 years** of diagnosis, most people with type 1 lose their **glucagon response** to hypoglycaemia. Injected insulin keeps working whatever the glucose level.

blocks.title: Symptoms
rows: Delirium, drowsiness, speech difficulty, poor concentration, incoordination, irritability; seizures and coma if severe
Children: behaviour change; older people: visual disturbance, ataxia

blocks.title: Losing the warning symptoms
items: **Impaired awareness of hypoglycaemia** affects about **20–25% of people with type 1**. Recurrent hypos lower the glucose level at which symptoms and counter-regulation start.
Long-standing **autonomic neuropathy** removes adrenergic warnings, and **β-blockers** can mask them.
These patients can slip into seizures or coma without warning. After severe hypoglycaemia, a looser HbA1c goal (< 8%) is reasonable.

blocks.title: Treating hypoglycaemia (Davidson)
rows: **10–15 g fast-acting carbohydrate**; recheck in 10–15 min; repeat if still < 4.0 mmol/L; then a longer-acting carbohydrate
IV **75–100 mL of 20% glucose** over 15 min, or **150–200 mL of 10%** over 15 min
After long-acting sulphonylurea or long-acting insulin
Expect recurrence: a **10% glucose infusion** titrated to glucose, or extra carbohydrate

blocks.text: **50% dextrose is no longer recommended** (Davidson), although US pocket texts still list D50. **Glucagon may work less well after a sulphonylurea or alcohol**, so be ready to give IV glucose.

blocks.title: Hypoglycaemia without diabetes therapy: insulin vs C-peptide

blocks.text: **Lactic acidosis** gives a **high anion gap metabolic acidosis**. **Type A** (Davidson: type 1) comes from **tissue hypoxia** (shock, circulatory failure). **Type B** (Davidson: type 2) comes from **impaired lactate metabolism** (liver disease, drugs such as **metformin**). Metformin-associated lactic acidosis is **rare**. It mostly follows overdose, or metformin continued despite **advanced renal or hepatic dysfunction**, and usually shows no marked hyperglycaemia or ketosis.
**Metformin and the kidney:** halve the dose at eGFR 30–45, stop it below 30, and withhold it during any acute illness that risks acute kidney injury. These rules prevent lactic acidosis.

sections.title: Chronic complications: eyes, kidneys, nerves and large vessels

blocks.text: **Microvascular disease** is marked by **capillary basement-membrane thickening** with leaky vessels. Its risk rises with the **duration and degree of hyperglycaemia**. **Macrovascular disease** (MI, stroke, peripheral arterial disease) causes most of the excess mortality: **cardiovascular disease causes ~70% of deaths**. CAD risk is roughly doubled, and **silent ischaemia** is common.

blocks.title: Diabetic retinopathy grading (Kumar Box 23.21)
rows: Cotton wool spots; hard exudates; dot (microaneurysm) and blot bleeds
**Venous beading/loops, IRMA**, multiple deep round haemorrhages
Exudates or haemorrhages near the macula ± reduced acuity

blocks.text: **Retinopathy mechanism and treatment:** capillary occlusion causes ischaemia, which drives **VEGF** release. VEGF causes leakage (microaneurysms, haemorrhages, exudates, **macular oedema**, the main cause of visual loss) and **new vessel** growth that can bleed or detach the retina. Proliferative disease → **pan-retinal laser photocoagulation**. Centre-involving macular oedema → **intravitreal anti-VEGF**.

blocks.note: Look at: blot haemorrhages, cotton wool spots, microaneurysms on fluorescein angiography, IRMA, venous beading and new vessels
Look at: microaneurysms and blot haemorrhages, hard exudates, new vessels on the disc, pre-retinal haemorrhage, exudative maculopathy, cataract against the red reflex

blocks.title: Diabetic nephropathy: albuminuria categories
rows: Men 2.5–30, women 3.5–30 mg/mmol; positive in 2 of 3 samples

blocks.title: Nephropathy key facts
items: About **30% of type 1** patients have nephropathy 20 years after diagnosis. It is the **leading cause of ESRD** in developed countries (20–50% of new RRT starts).
Natural history: **hyperfiltration → microalbuminuria → proteinuria (~10 y) → nephrotic range → ESRF**.
Histology: GBM thickening, mesangial expansion and the **Kimmelstiel–Wilson nodule** (nodular glomerulosclerosis, pathognomonic).

Treatment: **ACE inhibitor or ARB first** (efferent arteriolar dilatation cuts hyperfiltration); check **K⁺ and creatinine** after starting; then add a diuretic and salt restriction. US texts add an **SGLT2 inhibitor** in type 2. Halving albuminuria nearly halves the risk of ESRD.

blocks.note: Look at: nodular diabetic glomerulosclerosis — thickened basement membrane, mesangial expansion and a Kimmelstiel–Wilson nodule

blocks.text: **Screen for nephropathy with the urine ACR, not a dipstick.** A standard dipstick turns positive only at overt proteinuria, when glycaemic control no longer meaningfully slows progression.

blocks.title: Diabetic neuropathy (Davidson Boxes 20.40–20.41)
rows: "Glove and stocking", feet first; lost ankle reflexes; painful in 15–30%
Proximal leg weakness and wasting, severe anterior leg pain, weight loss
**CN III (pupil-sparing) and VI**, femoral, sciatic; carpal tunnel entrapment
Postural hypotension, resting tachycardia, **gastroparesis**, nocturnal diarrhoea, atonic bladder, erectile dysfunction, gustatory sweating

blocks.title: Neuropathy treatment (Davidson Box 20.43)
rows: Better glycaemic control; **gabapentin/pregabalin**, **amitriptyline**, **duloxetine**, topical capsaicin, opiates (tramadol)

blocks.text: Neuropathy affects **50–90%** of people with diabetes, depending on the definition. Once autonomic symptoms are overt, **30–50% die within 10 years**.

Foot ulcers follow **often trivial trauma** to a **neuropathic and/or ischaemic** foot, typically under **callus**. Ischaemia alone causes only a minority; most are **neuropathic or neuro-ischaemic**. Lost sensation lets injuries go unnoticed, and poor blood flow stops them healing.

blocks.title: Annual foot screening
items: **10 g monofilament** at five points on each foot (avoid callus). Feeling **fewer than 8 of 10 touches** raises ulcer risk **5–10-fold**.
Palpate **dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial** pulses.
Inspect for callus, deformity, clawing, fungal infection and ulcers.

blocks.title: Managing an ulcer
items: Refer to a **multidisciplinary foot team** (diabetologist, podiatrist, vascular surgeon, orthotist).
**Débride** dead tissue; give **antibiotics** promptly if infected.
**Off-load** pressure (casts, special footwear).
**Revascularise** if neuro-ischaemic.

blocks.text: **Acute Charcot neuroarthropathy** presents as a **hot, red, swollen foot** in a patient with neuropathy, and is easily mistaken for cellulitis or osteomyelitis. The **first X-ray is often normal**; **MRI** helps. Treat with **immobilisation in a total contact cast** and avoid weight-bearing. Late deformity gives a **"rocker-bottom" foot**.
Neuropathy can **mask claudication**, and **medial arterial calcification** makes leg arteries stiff, which **falsely raises** ankle blood pressure readings.

blocks.title: Foot-care education (prevention)
items: Inspect and wash the feet **daily**; moisturise dry skin; change socks daily.
Cut nails regularly; **never walk barefoot**; check shoes for foreign objects; wear well-fitting shoes.
Do not burst blisters or use over-the-counter corn remedies; cover minor cuts with sterile dressings.

blocks.title: Skin and injection-site signs
items: **Necrobiosis lipoidica**, granuloma annulare, bullae, pigmentation, vitiligo, xanthelasma.
**Acanthosis nigricans**: a marker of insulin resistance.
**Lipohypertrophy** from repeated injection into one site causes erratic insulin absorption. Check sites in an unexpectedly poor responder and teach site rotation.
Serious infections linked to diabetes include **mucormycosis** and **necrotising (malignant) otitis externa**.

blocks.note: Look at: clawed toes, plantar callus, neuropathic ulcer, digital gangrene, Charcot "rocker-bottom" X-ray, superficial femoral artery occlusion on angiogram
Look at: high arch with clawing, a typical plantar neuropathic ulcer, and the distribution of ischaemic ulcers
Look at: a neuropathic diabetic foot ulcer

sections.title: Long-term management: targets, oral agents and insulin

blocks.title: Individualised targets
rows: Early type 2 on diet or 1–2 oral agents
Older, cardiovascular disease, or on insulin with hypoglycaemia risk
HbA1c < 7% for most; < 6.5% if hypo risk low; ≤ 8% if frail or severe hypos
Statin for most type 2 patients over 40
HbA1c every 3–6 months; annual ACR, eye screening and lipids; feet and BP every visit

blocks.text: **Type 2 stepwise treatment** starts with **lifestyle plus metformin**. If the HbA1c target is not met after about 3 months, add a **second agent** (sulphonylurea, pioglitazone, DPP-4 inhibitor, SGLT2 inhibitor, GLP-1 receptor agonist or basal insulin), then a third, then injectables. **Start insulin early** if glucose is very high or the patient is symptomatic and catabolic. **Type 1 always needs insulin.**

**Guideline age matters.** Davidson 24e follows ADA/EASD 2015, written before the cardiovascular outcome trials. Newer US practice (Pocket) gives a **GLP-1 RA first with established or high-risk ASCVD**, and an **SGLT2 inhibitor first with heart failure or proteinuric CKD**, whatever the HbA1c. Davidson already notes these classes are likely to move earlier.

blocks.note: Look at: metformin → dual → triple therapy → injectables, with each class's efficacy, hypoglycaemia risk, weight effect and side-effects

blocks.title: Glucose-lowering drugs
rows: GI upset (~25%); rare lactic acidosis; halve dose at eGFR 30–45, stop < 30
Close β-cell KATP channels → insulin release
**Fluid retention, heart failure**, fractures, possible bladder cancer
Well tolerated; pancreatitis; heart-failure signal with saxagliptin
**Genital fungal infections**, dehydration, rare **euglycaemic DKA**; empagliflozin cut CV death by 35%

blocks.title: Insulin regimens
items: **Type 1**: **basal-bolus** (long-acting once or twice daily plus rapid-acting with meals) or an insulin **pump**. Total needs are usually 0.5–1.0 U/kg/day.
**Type 2**: usually **once-daily long-acting insulin added to oral agents**.
**Twice-daily premixed**: about two-thirds of the dose in the morning (short:intermediate 1:2).
Side-effects: **hypoglycaemia, weight gain, lipohypertrophy**.

blocks.note: Look at: the onset, peak and duration curves of rapid, short, intermediate and long-acting insulins

blocks.text: **Dawn phenomenon**: fasting hyperglycaemia from early-morning **GH and cortisol** plus waning overnight isophane. It is **not** rebound from nocturnal hypoglycaemia; the old "Somogyi effect" has been refuted. Only **night-time glucose testing** confirms nocturnal hypos.

**In hospital, never stop basal insulin in type 1.** Without it DKA develops, and sliding-scale insulin alone is inadequate. When nil by mouth, type 2 patients usually get a reduced basal dose and no prandial doses.

sections.title: Prevention of diabetes and its complications

blocks.title: Preventing type 2 in people at risk (IGT / pre-diabetes)
items: **Lifestyle** works best: weight loss, less (saturated) fat, more fibre, and about **30 minutes of moderate activity daily**. Diet and exercise cut progression by about **58%**.
**Metformin** (about **31%**) and **orlistat** also lower incidence, but less than lifestyle. Keep them for people who cannot change lifestyle or whose glucose keeps rising.
Explain the **risk of progression**, and control **cardiovascular risk factors** (BP, lipids) aggressively.
**Bariatric surgery** can normalise glucose and cause remission.

blocks.text: **Type 2 can remit with weight loss.** In the DiRECT trial, an **800 kcal/day** diet put many patients into remission. Pre-diabetes is managed with education and lifestyle change rather than drugs.

blocks.title: Landmark trials of glycaemic control
rows: Intensive control cut complications by about **60%** (Kumar: 60% for retinopathy, less for nephropathy and neuropathy) but **tripled severe hypoglycaemia**
Each 11 mmol/mol (1%) fall in HbA1c → **21% fewer diabetes deaths, 14% fewer MIs, 30–40% less microvascular disease**
Tight control clearly prevents **microvascular** disease; macrovascular benefit is less certain

blocks.text: **Do not chase strict targets in frail, older patients** with long-standing diabetes and cardiovascular disease. ACCORD showed harm, and hypoglycaemia risk outweighs benefit, so aim nearer 58 mmol/mol.

blocks.title: Preventing complications in established diabetes
items: Glucose, **BP** and **lipid** control (statin), and stopping smoking.
**Annual** retinal screening, urine ACR and foot risk assessment, with ACE inhibitor/ARB for albuminuria.
Daily **foot-care** education.

cards.front: Glucokinase (GCK) MODY: typical picture and treatment?
cards.back: Mild, stable fasting hyperglycaemia (altered glucose set-point), autosomal dominant; usually **needs no treatment**.

cards.front: Ketosis-prone ("Flatbush") type 2 diabetes?
cards.back: Presents in **DKA** (classically described in African American people); insulin at first, but β cells often recover so **metformin can replace insulin after ~3 months**.

cards.front: Type 1 risk for a child: father vs mother affected?
cards.back: **Father ~10%**; mother 1–4%; both parents up to 30%.

cards.front: β-cell loss when type 1 becomes overt vs at type 2 diagnosis?
cards.back: Type 1: **80–90%** of function lost. Type 2: about **50%** lost at diagnosis.

cards.front: Common gene variant with the largest effect on type 2 risk?
What is the "prayer sign" in diabetes?
cards.back: **Cheiroarthropathy** (limited joint mobility): the palms cannot be pressed flat together.

cards.front: What proportion of people with type 2 already have complications at diagnosis?
Diagnostic thresholds for diabetes (SI)?
cards.back: Fasting ≥ **7.0** mmol/L; random or 2-h OGTT ≥ **11.1** mmol/L; HbA1c ≥ **48** mmol/mol. Asymptomatic patients need two results.

cards.front: IFG vs IGT definitions?
cards.back: **IFG**: fasting 6.1 to < 7.0 mmol/L. **IGT**: fasting < 7.0 with 2-h OGTT **7.8–11.1** mmol/L.

cards.front: What does C-peptide measure, and why is it useful?
cards.back: Endogenous insulin secretion, measurable even on injected insulin: very low in long-standing type 1, very high in insulin resistance.

cards.front: DKA diagnostic criteria (Davidson/JBDS)?
cards.back: Ketones ≥ **3.0** mmol/L (or urine > 2+), glucose ≥ **11** mmol/L, and bicarbonate < **15** mmol/L and/or venous pH < **7.3**.

cards.front: Name four markers of severe DKA.
cards.back: Any of: ketones > 6, bicarbonate < 5, pH < 7.0, admission K⁺ < 3.5, GCS < 12, SpO₂ < 92%, SBP < 90, pulse > 100 or < 60, anion gap > 16.

cards.front: HHS criteria?
cards.back: Hypovolaemia, glucose **> 30 mmol/L**, osmolality **> 320 mOsmol/kg**, ketones < 3 mmol/L, pH > 7.3, bicarbonate > 15 mmol/L.

cards.front: In DKA, when is glucose added to the drip?
cards.back: When glucose falls **< 14 mmol/L**: 10% glucose 125 mL/hr, while saline and fixed-rate insulin continue.

cards.front: Unconscious hypoglycaemia with IV access: what dose?
cards.back: IV **75–100 mL of 20%** (or 150–200 mL of 10%) glucose over 15 min; IM glucagon 1 mg if no access. 50% dextrose is no longer recommended.

cards.front: Hypoglycaemia with high insulin but low C-peptide?
cards.back: **Factitious (exogenous) insulin**. Insulinoma and sulphonylureas raise both.

cards.front: Microalbuminuria by ACR (Davidson)?
cards.back: Men **2.5–30**, women **3.5–30** mg/mmol, in 2 of 3 early-morning samples. > 30 mg/mmol = overt nephropathy.

cards.front: Pathognomonic renal lesion of diabetes?
cards.back: **Kimmelstiel–Wilson nodule** (nodular glomerulosclerosis).

cards.front: Retinal features of pre-proliferative (R2) retinopathy?
cards.back: **Venous beading/loops**, **IRMA**, multiple deep round haemorrhages; non-urgent referral.

cards.front: Monofilament result that predicts foot ulcers?
cards.back: Feeling **< 8 of 10** touches (5 sites per foot) → **5–10-fold** higher ulcer risk.

cards.front: Acute Charcot foot: presentation and treatment?
cards.back: Hot, red, swollen foot with often normal first X-ray (MRI helps). **Total contact cast**, no weight-bearing.

cards.front: Metformin dose rules by eGFR?
cards.back: **Halve** the dose at eGFR 30–45; **stop** below 30; withhold in acute illness.

cards.front: Duration of long-acting analogues (glargine, detemir, degludec)?
Typical adverse effects of SGLT2 inhibitors?
cards.back: Genital fungal infections, dehydration, weight loss, rare **euglycaemic DKA**.

cards.front: Prevention in pre-diabetes: lifestyle vs metformin?
cards.back: Diet and exercise cut progression by about **58%**; metformin by about **31%**.

cards.front: UKPDS: benefit of an 11 mmol/mol (1%) HbA1c fall?
cards.back: 21% fewer diabetes deaths, 14% fewer MIs, 30–40% less microvascular disease.

questions.leadIn: Pick the best option for each scenario. Some options will be used more than once and some not at all.
options: MODY due to a glucokinase mutation
MODY due to an HNF1-alpha mutation
MODY due to an HNF1-beta mutation

items.stem: A 23-year-old woman of normal weight has had fasting plasma glucose readings of 6.6–7.3 mmol/L at every annual check for 6 years, with no change. Her mother and maternal grandmother were told they had "slightly high sugar" but never took treatment. Islet antibodies are negative, and there is no retinopathy.
items.explanation: Lifelong, **stable, mild fasting hyperglycaemia** that does not progress, in an autosomal-dominant pattern, is typical of **glucokinase MODY**. It usually needs no treatment.

items.stem: A 39-year-old man of African-Caribbean origin with a BMI of 34 kg/m² is admitted in diabetic ketoacidosis. GAD and IA-2 antibodies are negative. Four months after discharge, he has been switched from insulin to metformin and his HbA1c remains 47 mmol/mol.
items.explanation: He presented in **DKA**, but he is obese and antibody-negative, and he came off insulin within months. That fits **ketosis-prone (Flatbush) type 2** diabetes, where β-cell function recovers.

items.stem: A 46-year-old slim woman was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes 14 months ago and has never been ketotic. Her HbA1c rose rapidly despite metformin and then gliclazide, and she now needs insulin. GAD antibodies are present at a high titre.
items.explanation: Two steps: an adult who **did not need insulin at first** (so not classic type 1), but who has **high-titre GAD antibodies** and **progressed rapidly to insulin**. That is **LADA**.

questions.stem: A man aged 61 who has type 2 diabetes for 8 years has had a capillary glucose of 18–24 mmol/L for 3 weeks while taking metformin. He is thirsty but not vomiting. His blood ketone level is 0.4 mmol/L and venous pH is 7.39.
questions.leadIn: Which mechanism best explains why he has not developed ketoacidosis?
options: The liver cannot make ketones in type 2 diabetes
Low residual insulin is enough to suppress lipolysis
Glucagon secretion is suppressed in type 2 diabetes
High free fatty acid levels inhibit hepatic ketogenesis
Renal SGLT2 transporters excrete ketones in the urine
questions.explanation: Suppressing **lipolysis** needs much less insulin than controlling glucose. The residual insulin in type 2 keeps FFA delivery to the liver low, so ketogenesis stays limited even when glucose is high.
whyNot: Wrong: the liver can make ketones in type 2, as ketosis-prone type 2 diabetes presenting in DKA shows.
Wrong: glucagon is actually **increased** in type 2 diabetes and contributes to hyperglycaemia.
Wrong: FFAs are the **substrate** for hepatic ketogenesis, so more FFA would promote ketosis, not prevent it.
Wrong: SGLT2 **reabsorbs filtered glucose** in the proximal tubule; it does not excrete ketones.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man has had type 1 diabetes since age 11. His partner does not have diabetes. They are planning a child and ask about the risk of the child developing type 1 diabetes.
questions.leadIn: What is the approximate lifetime risk for the child?
questions.explanation: When the **father** has type 1, the risk to a child is about **10%**, higher than when the mother is affected (1–4%). Most new cases (80–85%) still have no family history.
whyNot: This is the risk when the **mother** has type 1.
This is the risk for an HLA-identical sibling.
This is the concordance for an identical twin.
No first-degree relationship carries this risk; even with both parents affected it is up to about 30%.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old student has 3 weeks of thirst, nocturia and 5 kg weight loss. He also says his distance vision has become blurred over the last week. Random plasma glucose is 24 mmol/L. Fundoscopy is normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause of his blurred vision?
questions.explanation: In acute hyperglycaemia, osmotic changes make the **lens swell** and alter its refraction, so vision blurs. It settles as glucose comes down. Fundoscopy is normal here.
whyNot: Maculopathy is a chronic microvascular complication that takes years to develop; complications are not expected at type 1 diagnosis and the fundus is normal.
New vessels and vitreous haemorrhage reflect long-standing proliferative retinopathy, and fundoscopy would be abnormal.
Cataract is a chronic change and would not appear over a week with a 3-week history.
A third nerve palsy causes ptosis and diplopia, not blurred distance vision.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man with a BMI of 36 kg/m² and hypertension has an HbA1c of 56 mmol/mol on two occasions. On examination, the skin of his axillae and the back of his neck is dark, thickened and velvety.
questions.leadIn: Which condition does this skin finding most specifically indicate?
questions.explanation: Dark, velvety skin in the flexures is **acanthosis nigricans**, the skin marker of **insulin resistance**. It fits his obesity and new type 2 diabetes.
whyNot: Lipohypertrophy is a soft swelling at insulin injection sites, and he is not on insulin.
Necrobiosis lipoidica is a diabetes-related skin lesion, but it is not the flexural, velvety marker of insulin resistance.
Vitiligo is depigmentation, the opposite of this, and is associated with type 1 autoimmunity.
Autonomic neuropathy causes postural hypotension, gustatory sweating and gastroparesis, not flexural pigmentation.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best match from the list. An option may fit several patients, or none.
options: Diabetes confirmed on the results given
Possible diabetes: repeat a diagnostic test
HbA1c unsuitable: use plasma glucose / OGTT

items.stem: A 52-year-old asymptomatic woman has a fasting plasma glucose of 6.4 mmol/L. A 75 g OGTT gives a 2-hour value of 7.2 mmol/L.
items.explanation: Fasting 6.1 to < 7.0 mmol/L with a normal 2-hour value (< 7.8) is **impaired fasting glucose**. IGT would need a 2-hour value of 7.8–11.1.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man with no symptoms has an HbA1c of 51 mmol/mol on a routine health check. No other results are available.
items.explanation: One diagnostic result in an **asymptomatic** person is not enough. A second diagnostic test, ideally the same test, is needed to confirm.

items.stem: A 31-year-old man has had 4 weeks of thirst, polyuria and 6 kg weight loss. A laboratory random plasma glucose is 16.2 mmol/L.
items.explanation: With **classic symptoms**, a single random plasma glucose ≥ 11.1 mmol/L confirms diabetes. No repeat test is needed.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman at 26 weeks of pregnancy has a BMI of 35 kg/m² and a family history of type 2 diabetes. Her GP plans to check for diabetes with an HbA1c.
items.explanation: HbA1c reads **falsely low in pregnancy** and is not used for diagnosis then. The **OGTT** is the preferred test in pregnancy.

questions.leadIn: Pick the best option for each scenario. Some options will be used more than once and some not at all.
options: 0.9% sodium chloride 500 mL over 10–15 minutes, then reassess
Add 10% glucose 125 mL/hour alongside saline and insulin
Add potassium chloride 40 mmol to each litre of fluid
No potassium in the fluids; recheck shortly

items.stem: A woman aged 22 who has type 1 diabetes has vomited for 2 days. Ketones are 5.8 mmol/L, pH 7.12, glucose 29 mmol/L. Blood pressure is 82/48 mmHg and pulse 126/min. What is the first fluid step?
items.explanation: In DKA with **systolic BP < 90 mmHg**, give **500 mL of 0.9% saline over 10–15 minutes** and reassess. The standard 1 L over an hour is for SBP > 90.

items.stem: A 19-year-old man is 5 hours into DKA treatment on fixed-rate insulin and 0.9% saline. Glucose is now 12.4 mmol/L, ketones 2.3 mmol/L and pH 7.26. What change is needed?
items.explanation: Glucose is below 14 mmol/L but ketones have not cleared. **Add 10% glucose** so the fixed-rate insulin can continue to switch off ketogenesis without causing hypoglycaemia. Do not stop the insulin.

items.stem: A 26-year-old with DKA has a potassium of 5.9 mmol/L on admission. Saline and fixed-rate insulin have been started. What should be done about potassium in the next bag of fluid?
items.explanation: K⁺ **> 5.5 mmol/L** means no added potassium for now. He is still total-body depleted, so recheck soon: K⁺ will fall once insulin works.

items.stem: An 80-year-old woman has a glucose of 46 mmol/L, osmolality 362 mOsmol/kg, ketones 0.7 mmol/L and pH 7.36. After 3 hours of 0.9% saline with a good positive fluid balance, her glucose is falling by only 2 mmol/L per hour. What should be started?
items.explanation: Two steps: the picture is **HHS**, not DKA (low ketones, no acidosis), so saline comes first without insulin. Once glucose falls **< 5 mmol/L/hr despite adequate fluids**, add **low-dose insulin 0.05 U/kg/hr**.

questions.leadIn: Match every case to one option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several cases, or for none.
options: Oral fast-acting carbohydrate 10–15 g, recheck in 10–15 minutes
Admit for a continuous 10% glucose infusion
Relax glycaemic targets and avoid further hypoglycaemia
Measure insulin and C-peptide during a hypoglycaemic episode
Increase the evening basal insulin dose

items.stem: An 83-year-old man taking glibenclamide is found drowsy at home with a glucose of 2.0 mmol/L. He wakes after IV glucose in the emergency department. What is the next step?
items.explanation: **Glibenclamide is long-acting**, so hypoglycaemia will recur after the first correction. Admit him and run a **10% glucose infusion**.

items.stem: A man aged 27 who has type 1 diabetes is found unrousable at home by his partner. His glucose is 1.8 mmol/L. Paramedics have not yet arrived, and his partner has been trained to use the emergency kit kept in the fridge.
items.explanation: He is unconscious with no IV access, so a trained relative gives **IM glucagon 1 mg**. Oral treatment is unsafe when he cannot swallow.

items.stem: A 25-year-old healthcare assistant without diabetes has three episodes of confusion with glucose of 1.9–2.4 mmol/L, each relieved by glucose. Her sister has type 1 diabetes. What is the most useful next investigation?
items.explanation: Two steps: unexplained hypoglycaemia with **access to insulin** raises factitious hypoglycaemia. **Insulin and C-peptide** taken during an episode separate injected insulin (high insulin, **low C-peptide**) from insulinoma or sulphonylurea (both high).

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best match from the list. An option may fit several patients, or none.

items.stem: A woman aged 58 who has type 2 diabetes for 6 years attends retinal screening. Both retinas show scattered dot and blot haemorrhages and a few hard exudates well away from the macula. Visual acuity is 6/6 in each eye.
items.explanation: Dot/blot haemorrhages and exudates **away from the macula**, with normal acuity, are **background (R1)** retinopathy, managed with annual screening.

items.stem: A man aged 34 who has type 1 diabetes for 17 years has screening photographs showing venous beading and intraretinal microvascular abnormalities, but no new vessels.
items.explanation: **Venous beading and IRMA** without new vessels define **pre-proliferative (R2)** retinopathy, which needs a non-urgent ophthalmology referral.

items.stem: A man aged 44 who has type 1 diabetes for 15 years has early-morning urine albumin:creatinine ratios of 11 and 14 mg/mmol in two of three samples. Urine dipstick is negative for protein and eGFR is 92.
items.explanation: An ACR of 2.5–30 mg/mmol in men, positive in 2 of 3 samples, is **microalbuminuria**. The dipstick stays negative until overt (> 30 mg/mmol) nephropathy.

questions.stem: A man aged 62 who has type 2 diabetes for 20 years cannot feel a monofilament on either foot. He has had 10 days of a hot, red, swollen left midfoot with little pain. There is no ulcer or break in the skin. Foot pulses are bounding, and the foot X-ray is normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Immobilise in a total contact cast and avoid weight-bearing
Reassure him, as the normal X-ray excludes bone disease
questions.explanation: A hot, swollen, relatively painless foot in someone with **neuropathy**, with **no skin break**, is **acute Charcot neuroarthropathy** until proved otherwise. The early X-ray is often normal, and MRI helps. Treatment is **immobilisation (total contact cast) and no weight-bearing**.
whyNot: Cellulitis usually has a portal of entry such as an ulcer; Charcot is the classic mimic and antibiotics do not treat it.
Gout is a painful arthritis; a near-painless hot, swollen midfoot in a patient with dense neuropathy is the Charcot pattern.
Bounding pulses show the foot is not ischaemic; revascularisation is for neuro-ischaemic ulcers.
The first X-ray in acute Charcot is often normal; missing it leads to collapse and rocker-bottom deformity.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman who smokes has type 2 diabetes. She has a painful ulcer on the tip of her second toe. The foot is cool, the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses cannot be felt, and she is woken at night by foot pain.
questions.leadIn: What type of foot lesion is this?
questions.explanation: A **cold, pulseless foot** with **rest pain** and a **painful ulcer on a toe tip** is the ischaemic pattern. Neuropathic feet are warm with bounding pulses, and their ulcers are painless and plantar.
whyNot: Neuropathic ulcers are painless, plantar and under callus, on a warm foot with bounding pulses.
Charcot presents as a hot, swollen, deformed foot, not a cold pulseless one.
Necrobiosis lipoidica is a skin lesion, not an ulcer on a cold, pulseless foot.
Osteomyelitis complicates deep (often neuropathic) ulcers; nothing here points to bone infection, and the dominant clues are ischaemic.

questions.theme: Glucose-lowering drugs and their adverse effects
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best match from the list. An option may fit several patients, or none.

items.stem: A woman aged 59 who has type 2 diabetes started a third oral agent 4 months ago. Her HbA1c has improved and she has lost 3 kg, but she has had two episodes of vulvovaginal candidiasis.
items.explanation: Weight loss with **genital fungal infection** comes from the glycosuria caused by an **SGLT2 inhibitor**.

items.stem: A 64-year-old man added a tablet to metformin 6 months ago. He has gained 5 kg, has ankle oedema and is more breathless on exertion. He has had no hypoglycaemia.
items.explanation: Weight gain, **fluid retention and worsening heart failure** without hypoglycaemia point to the PPARγ agonist **pioglitazone**.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman on metformin started a once-daily injection 2 months ago. She has persistent nausea and has lost 6 kg.
items.explanation: An injectable that causes **nausea and weight loss** is a **GLP-1 receptor agonist** such as liraglutide.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man on metformin and a newer oral agent is admitted with 2 days of vomiting. pH is 7.11, blood ketones 5.4 mmol/L and glucose only 9.6 mmol/L.
items.explanation: Two steps: acidosis with high ketones but **near-normal glucose** is **euglycaemic DKA**, a rare but recognised effect of **SGLT2 inhibitors**.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man has a BMI of 31 kg/m². His fasting plasma glucose is 6.4 mmol/L and a 2-hour OGTT value is 9.1 mmol/L. He is keen to avoid diabetes.
questions.leadIn: Which intervention most effectively reduces his risk of progressing to type 2 diabetes?
options: Structured lifestyle change: weight loss, diet and about 30 minutes of daily activity
No intervention; repeat the OGTT in a year
questions.explanation: He has **IGT**. **Lifestyle change** reduces progression most (about 58%), more than metformin (about 31%) or orlistat. Drugs are kept for people who cannot change lifestyle or whose glucose keeps rising.
whyNot: Metformin lowers incidence but less than lifestyle change (about 31% vs 58%).
Orlistat reduces incidence but is less effective than lifestyle and is a second choice.
Sulphonylureas are not used to prevent diabetes; they cause weight gain and hypoglycaemia.
People with pre-diabetes should be told their risk and given lifestyle advice now, with cardiovascular risk factors controlled.

questions.stem: An 81-year-old woman has had type 2 diabetes for 24 years and had a myocardial infarction 3 years ago. She lives alone and is becoming frail. Her HbA1c is 60 mmol/mol on metformin and gliclazide. A junior doctor proposes adding basal insulin to bring her HbA1c below 48 mmol/mol.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Keep a relaxed target near 58 mmol/mol and avoid hypoglycaemia
Add basal insulin to reach an HbA1c below 48 mmol/mol
Aim for an HbA1c below 42 mmol/mol to prevent further MI
questions.explanation: For older patients with **cardiovascular disease** and hypoglycaemia risk, Davidson suggests an HbA1c **around 58 mmol/mol**. **ACCORD** found **higher mortality** when such patients were pushed below 48 mmol/mol.
whyNot: Intensifying to < 48 mmol/mol in an older patient with CVD raised mortality in ACCORD and increases hypoglycaemia.
Glibenclamide is long-acting and especially likely to cause hypoglycaemia; avoid it in older people.
This is stricter still and carries even more hypoglycaemia risk with no proven benefit.
Her HbA1c is near her individual target on current drugs; stopping all treatment risks symptomatic hyperglycaemia.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best match from the list. An option may fit several patients, or none.

items.stem: An 84-year-old care-home resident with type 2 diabetes has had 10 days of increasing confusion. Glucose is 51 mmol/L, sodium 151 mmol/L, osmolality 372 mOsmol/kg, ketones 0.8 mmol/L, pH 7.35 and bicarbonate 23 mmol/L.
items.explanation: Very high glucose and **osmolality > 320** with **no significant ketosis or acidosis**, developing over days in an older person, is **HHS**.

items.stem: A man aged 70 who has type 2 diabetes on metformin 1 g twice daily has had diarrhoea and vomiting for 3 days. eGFR is 21. pH is 7.04 with a high anion gap and raised lactate. Glucose is 8.1 mmol/L, ketones 0.4 mmol/L and blood pressure 124/76 mmHg.
items.explanation: High anion gap acidosis with raised lactate, **little hyperglycaemia or ketosis**, and **metformin continued despite severe renal impairment** is metformin-associated (type B) lactic acidosis. BP is normal, so tissue hypoxia (type A) is unlikely.

items.stem: A woman aged 24 who has type 1 diabetes has influenza and has been vomiting. Glucose is 27 mmol/L, ketones 5.2 mmol/L, pH 7.17 and bicarbonate 9 mmol/L.
items.explanation: Ketones ≥ 3, glucose ≥ 11 and bicarbonate < 15 / pH < 7.3 meet the criteria for **DKA**, precipitated by infection.

items.stem: A 20-year-old man treated for DKA with 6 L of 0.9% saline over 20 hours now has ketones of 0.2 mmol/L and glucose 9 mmol/L. His bicarbonate is 16 mmol/L, chloride is high and the anion gap is normal.
items.explanation: Two steps: the ketosis has **resolved** (ketones < 0.3), so the persisting low bicarbonate is not ongoing DKA. With a **normal anion gap and high chloride** after large saline volumes, it is **hyperchloraemic acidosis**.

questions.stem: A man aged 28 who has type 1 diabetes is admitted with DKA. Results: glucose 34 mmol/L, ketones 4.6 mmol/L, potassium 5.2 mmol/L, white cell count 18 × 10⁹/L, pH 6.94. Temperature is 36.9°C.
questions.leadIn: Which result most clearly marks this as severe DKA?
questions.explanation: A **pH below 7.0** is one of Davidson's markers of severe DKA (with ketones > 6, bicarbonate < 5, admission K⁺ < 3.5, low GCS, hypotension and others). It calls for senior and high-dependency review.
whyNot: Glucose level does **not** reflect DKA severity; DKA can even occur with near-normal glucose.
A high-normal admission K⁺ is common; only K⁺ < 3.5 mmol/L on admission marks severity.
Leucocytosis is a stress response in DKA and does not by itself indicate severity or infection.
Fever may be absent even with infection; a normal temperature is not a severity marker.

questions.stem: A diabetes clinic is reviewing which patients can have diabetes diagnosed by HbA1c alone.
questions.leadIn: In which patient is HbA1c an acceptable diagnostic test?
options: An 8-year-old boy with 2 weeks of polyuria and weight loss
A 30-year-old woman at 28 weeks of pregnancy
A 55-year-old asymptomatic obese man with a normal full blood count
A 47-year-old woman with sickle cell disease
questions.explanation: HbA1c suits **slow-onset, asymptomatic** hyperglycaemia when red cell turnover is normal. The other patients have suspected type 1, pregnancy, a haemoglobinopathy or uraemia.
whyNot: Suspected type 1 / rapid-onset symptomatic hyperglycaemia: HbA1c lags behind and should not be used; measure plasma glucose.
HbA1c is falsely low in pregnancy; use an OGTT.
Haemoglobinopathies make HbA1c unreliable.
Uraemia makes HbA1c difficult to interpret.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old woman was diagnosed with diabetes at 18 and started on insulin. She needs only 10 units a day and has never had ketosis. Her father and paternal grandmother had diabetes diagnosed in their twenties. Islet autoantibodies are negative.
questions.leadIn: Which test best shows whether she still produces her own insulin?
questions.explanation: **C-peptide** is cleaved from pro-insulin, so it measures **endogenous** insulin secretion even in someone injecting insulin. Preserved C-peptide years after diagnosis argues against type 1 and, with this family history, points to **MODY**.
whyNot: HbA1c measures average glycaemia, not insulin secretion.
Fasting glucose shows control, not whether her β cells still work.
An OGTT diagnoses glucose intolerance; it does not separate endogenous from injected insulin.
Urine ketones (acetoacetate only) say nothing about endogenous insulin, and their absence does not exclude type 1.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman has had type 1 diabetes for 16 years and keeps tight control (HbA1c 45 mmol/mol). Twice this month colleagues have found her confused, with glucose of 2.1 and 2.4 mmol/L. She had no sweating, tremor or hunger beforehand. She takes no other medicines.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely explanation for the lack of warning symptoms?
options: Impaired awareness of hypoglycaemia from recurrent hypoglycaemia
questions.explanation: Long-standing type 1 with **tight control and frequent hypos** lowers the glucose level at which warning symptoms start. That is **impaired awareness**, which affects about 20–25% of people with type 1. Hypoglycaemia must be strictly avoided, and after severe hypos a looser HbA1c goal is reasonable.
whyNot: She takes no other medicines, so a β-blocker cannot be masking symptoms.
She has type 1 and injects insulin, which explains the hypos; nothing suggests an insulinoma.
The Somogyi effect describes rebound morning hyperglycaemia and has been refuted; it does not explain absent warnings.
Nothing points to secret drug use; recurrent hypos from her own insulin explain the picture.

questions.stem: A woman aged 21 who has type 1 diabetes presents with DKA: glucose 31 mmol/L, ketones 5.9 mmol/L, pH 7.08, bicarbonate 7 mmol/L and potassium **3.1 mmol/L**. Blood pressure is 104/62 mmHg.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate way to handle her potassium?
options: Run fluids and insulin with no added potassium
Add 40 mmol/L potassium chloride as per the standard regimen
Seek senior review and give additional potassium beyond the standard 40 mmol/L, with cardiac monitoring
Give IV sodium bicarbonate to correct the acidosis first
Double the insulin infusion rate to clear ketones faster
questions.explanation: **Step 1:** Everyone in DKA is **total-body K⁺ depleted**, and insulin will drive K⁺ into cells. **Step 2:** An admission K⁺ **below 3.5 mmol/L** is itself a marker of **severe DKA**. **Step 3:** Davidson's table gives no K⁺ above 5.5, **40 mmol/L for 3.5–5.5**, and **senior review with extra potassium** below 3.5, with ECG monitoring in severe cases. (US texts go further and **hold insulin until K⁺ > 3.3**.)
whyNot: With K⁺ already low, insulin would cause dangerous hypokalaemia; potassium must be added.
The standard 40 mmol/L is for K⁺ 3.5–5.5 mmol/L; at 3.1 more is needed with senior input.
Bicarbonate is not recommended in DKA, and correcting acidosis shifts potassium into cells, lowering it further.
The insulin rate is fixed at 0.1 U/kg/hr; more insulin would push K⁺ down further.

questions.stem: A man aged 79 who has type 2 diabetes on gliclazide is brought in with 6 days of increasing drowsiness after a chest infection. Glucose is 44 mmol/L, sodium 149 mmol/L, urea 19 mmol/L, calculated osmolality 360 mOsmol/kg, ketones 0.6 mmol/L and pH 7.34.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
options: 0.9% sodium chloride 1 L over the first hour, without insulin initially
0.45% sodium chloride 1 L over the first hour
questions.explanation: **Step 1, classify:** glucose > 30, osmolality > 320, ketones < 3 and pH > 7.3 make this **HHS**, not DKA. **Step 2, fluid first:** HHS is mainly a profound water and salt deficit, so start **0.9% saline alone**, aiming for an osmolality fall of 3–8 mOsmol/kg/hr. Fluid by itself lowers glucose. **Step 3, insulin later:** start **0.05 U/kg/hr** only if ketones are > 1.0 mmol/L, or if glucose falls < 5 mmol/L/hr despite adequate fluids. Also give LMWH prophylaxis and treat the infection.
whyNot: Early full-dose insulin in HHS drops glucose and osmolality too fast, shifting water into cells; insulin is low-dose and delayed unless ketotic.
0.45% saline is kept for osmolality that keeps rising despite adequate 0.9% saline, not for the start.
Glucose is 44 mmol/L; glucose is only added once it falls below about 14 mmol/L.
He is not acidotic, and bicarbonate has no role.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man with a BMI of 33 kg/m² was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes 3 months ago. Despite diet and exercise his HbA1c is 62 mmol/mol. eGFR is 78, and he has no cardiovascular, renal or heart failure history.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate first drug?
options: Metformin, started at a low dose and titrated
questions.explanation: **Step 1:** Lifestyle measures alone have not reached target after about 3 months, so a drug is needed. **Step 2:** **Metformin** is first-line. It is weight-neutral, causes no hypoglycaemia, and his eGFR allows the full dose. Start low (500 mg once or twice daily) to limit GI upset, then build up. **Step 3:** If the target is still unmet, add a second agent. In patients with established ASCVD, heart failure or proteinuric CKD, newer guidance uses a GLP-1 RA or SGLT2 inhibitor early.
whyNot: A sulphonylurea is a second-line add-on; it causes weight gain and hypoglycaemia in an already obese man.
Pioglitazone is second-line and causes weight gain and fluid retention.
Insulin is for severe hyperglycaemia or failure of other agents; an HbA1c of 62 does not need it first.
DPP-4 inhibitors are second-line add-ons to metformin.

questions.leadIn: Match every case to one option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several cases, or for none.

items.stem: A 73-year-old man with no family history of diabetes is found to have an HbA1c of 64 mmol/mol. He has lost 9 kg over 3 months and has a poor appetite.
items.explanation: New diabetes in an **older person with weight loss and anorexia** should prompt a search for **pancreatic carcinoma**.

items.stem: A 56-year-old man has drunk heavily for 30 years. He has recurrent epigastric pain radiating to the back, pale floating stools, and pancreatic calcification on CT. His glucose is now persistently high.
items.explanation: Pain, **steatorrhoea** and **pancreatic calcification** in a heavy drinker point to **chronic pancreatitis**, an often-missed cause of diabetes that usually needs insulin.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman has new diabetes, chronic diarrhoea and an unprovoked deep vein thrombosis. Imaging shows a pancreatic tail mass.
items.explanation: The "**3 Ds**" (diabetes, DVT, diarrhoea) with a pancreatic mass suggest a **glucagonoma**.

items.stem: A 48-year-old man has hepatomegaly, abnormal liver tests, grey-bronze skin, a very high transferrin saturation and new diabetes.
items.explanation: Two steps: **iron overload** (high transferrin saturation) with liver disease and pigmentation is **haemochromatosis**, where iron deposits in the pancreas cause diabetes.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best match from the list. An option may fit several patients, or none.

items.stem: The insulin made up as 50 units in 50 mL of 0.9% saline for a fixed-rate intravenous infusion in DKA.
items.explanation: **Soluble (regular) insulin** is the preparation used intravenously.

items.stem: A cloudy insulin that must be mixed before injection. It starts working in 1–3 hours, peaks at 3–8 hours and lasts about 7–14 hours.
items.explanation: Cloudy, with a peak and an intermediate duration: **isophane (NPH)** insulin.

items.stem: A 4-month-old girl has needed insulin since 3 weeks of age. Genetic testing shows an activating mutation in the KIR6.2 subunit of the β-cell KATP channel. What treatment could replace her insulin?
items.explanation: Two steps: this is **permanent neonatal diabetes** caused by a **KATP-channel** mutation. Sulphonylureas close that channel, and over 90% of these patients can switch to **oral sulphonylureas**.

questions.stem: A woman aged 33 who has type 1 diabetes on a basal-bolus regimen has fasting glucose of 13–15 mmol/L every morning. Her bedtime readings are 7–8 mmol/L, and she has no symptoms overnight.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Check her glucose at about 03:00 to look for nocturnal hypoglycaemia
Increase her evening basal insulin immediately
Reduce her evening basal insulin because this is the Somogyi effect
questions.explanation: Morning hyperglycaemia may be the **dawn phenomenon** (early-morning GH and cortisol, waning overnight insulin). Nocturnal hypoglycaemia can only be found by **night-time glucose testing**. Check overnight before changing the basal dose.
whyNot: Raising basal insulin without excluding nocturnal hypoglycaemia could make undetected night hypos worse.
The Somogyi effect (rebound after nocturnal hypos) has been refuted; do not assume it.
Metformin is not the standard answer to fasting hyperglycaemia in type 1.
Breakfast insulin covers the post-breakfast rise, not the fasting level before it.

questions.stem: A woman aged 68 who has type 2 diabetes takes metformin 1 g twice daily. Her eGFR has fallen to 38 mL/min/1.73 m² and is stable. She is well.
questions.leadIn: What should be done with her metformin?
questions.explanation: At **eGFR 30–45**, the metformin dose is **reduced (halved)**. It is **stopped below 30**, and withheld during acute illness, to limit the risk of lactic acidosis.
whyNot: Stopping is for eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m².
Full dose at eGFR 38 increases accumulation and lactic acidosis risk.
Increasing the dose is unsafe with reduced renal function.
Glibenclamide is long-acting and causes hypoglycaemia; avoid it in older people.

questions.stem: A man aged 41 who has type 1 diabetes for 19 years has early-morning ACRs of 17 and 22 mg/mmol. Blood pressure is 138/84 mmHg, potassium 4.5 mmol/L and creatinine normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Start an ACE inhibitor and recheck potassium and creatinine
Repeat ACR in a year and treat only if the dipstick becomes positive
questions.explanation: He has **microalbuminuria**. An **ACE inhibitor (or ARB)** is first-line because it dilates the **efferent arteriole** and cuts hyperfiltration. Check **K⁺ and creatinine** after starting. Halving albuminuria nearly halves the risk of ESRD.
whyNot: Diuretics are second-line add-ons after ACEi/ARB.
β-blockers do not target the glomerular hyperfiltration that drives diabetic nephropathy.
Waiting for dipstick proteinuria wastes the window when treatment works best.
Other antihypertensives are add-ons; renin–angiotensin blockade is first-line.

questions.leadIn: Pick the best option for each scenario. Some options will be used more than once and some not at all.

items.stem: A woman aged 49 who has type 1 diabetes for 28 years has early satiety and vomits undigested food several hours after meals. Her glucose has become erratic. Endoscopy shows no obstruction.
items.explanation: **Gastroparesis** from autonomic neuropathy is treated with a **dopamine antagonist** (metoclopramide or domperidone); erythromycin is an alternative.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man with long-standing diabetes feels faint when he stands up. His BP is 142/80 mmHg lying and 104/66 mmHg standing, with no rise in heart rate. Support stockings alone have not helped.
items.explanation: **Postural hypotension** from autonomic neuropathy: support stockings first, then **fludrocortisone**.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man with autonomic neuropathy has recurrent urinary infections. A bladder scan shows 450 mL of residual urine after voiding.
items.explanation: An **atonic (neurogenic) bladder** with a large residual volume is managed with **intermittent self-catheterisation**.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man has burning pain in both feet that is worse at night, in a stocking distribution. Monofilament sensation is reduced and ankle reflexes are absent. Paracetamol has not helped.
items.explanation: Two steps: this is painful **distal symmetrical sensory neuropathy**. Davidson lists anticonvulsants (**pregabalin**, gabapentin), tricyclics and duloxetine as the main oral options.

questions.stem: Five patients with diabetes have the following blood results (glucose and ketones in mmol/L).
questions.leadIn: Which set of results meets the diagnostic criteria for diabetic ketoacidosis?
questions.explanation: DKA needs all three: **ketones ≥ 3.0**, **glucose ≥ 11** and **acidosis** (bicarbonate < 15 and/or pH < 7.3). Only option B has all three.
whyNot: Hyperglycaemia with mild ketosis but no acidosis: not DKA.
Very high glucose and osmolality without ketoacidosis: HHS.
Acidosis with high lactate and no ketosis: lactic acidosis.
Low glucose with normal acid–base: hypoglycaemia.

questions.theme: Choosing the right test in diabetes
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best match from the list. An option may fit several patients, or none.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman at 25 weeks of pregnancy has a BMI of 36 kg/m² and had a large baby in her last pregnancy. Which test should be used to look for diabetes?
items.explanation: HbA1c is unreliable in pregnancy. The **OGTT** is the preferred diagnostic test.

items.stem: A man aged 60 who has type 2 diabetes for 4 years has his annual review. Urine dipstick is negative for protein. Which test screens for early diabetic kidney disease?
items.explanation: An **early-morning urine ACR** detects microalbuminuria long before a dipstick turns positive.

items.stem: A 57-year-old man with neuropathy has a deep plantar ulcer and a warm, swollen midfoot. His X-ray is unhelpful. Which test best distinguishes Charcot neuroarthropathy from osteomyelitis?
items.explanation: Two steps: a hot swollen foot **with an ulcer** could be Charcot or osteomyelitis, and the early X-ray often cannot tell them apart. **MRI** is the most helpful test.

ospe.identify: Natural history of type 1: genetic susceptibility + environmental trigger → insulitis → autoantibodies → loss of first-phase insulin release → IGT → overt diabetes as β-cell mass falls
Acanthosis nigricans (insulin resistance), the prayer sign (cheiroarthropathy), necrobiosis lipoidica on the shins, and lipohypertrophy at injection sites
Background retinopathy (blot haemorrhages, cotton wool spots), IRMA and venous beading (pre-proliferative) and new vessels (proliferative)
Exudative maculopathy (hard exudates near the fovea), new vessels on the disc, and boat-shaped pre-retinal haemorrhage
Kimmelstiel–Wilson nodule: nodular glomerulosclerosis with mesangial expansion, pathognomonic of diabetic nephropathy
Neuropathic plantar ulcer under callus, clawed toes, digital gangrene, and the rocker-bottom deformity of Charcot neuroarthropathy on X-ray
Neuropathic foot (high arch, clawed toes, painless plantar ulcer) vs ischaemic ulcers on the toes and heel margins
